The Other Guy’s Brake Pads

How the ability to stop made speed possible.

By Theo Wren · 29 minute read

There may be no better scene in cinema about brakes than Chris Farley explaining what happens when you use the “other guy’s” brake pads in Tommy Boy. If you do not know what I am talking about, stop reading this article, find Tommy Boy on one of the approximately 12 streaming services you apparently need to subscribe to now, watch the scene, remember it, and then come back. I’ll wait.

For everyone else, you know exactly what happens. Tommy Callahan is trying to sell brake pads, the customer is not particularly interested and technical explanations are getting nowhere, so Tommy reaches for the customer’s prized model cars and decides to demonstrate the difference between good brake pads and bad brake pads in the only way Tommy Callahan knows how: by turning a perfectly ordinary sales presentation into a horrifying miniature traffic accident involving a family, fire and emergency personnel. The presentation is disastrous, but the lesson is perfect. Brakes matter.

And beneath all the Chris Farley insanity is actually one of the most fundamental principles in transportation: being able to go fast is useless unless you have an equally convincing way of slowing down.

Speed is wonderful. It is exciting, it is intoxicating, and human beings have spent virtually our entire existence figuring out how to move faster—faster horses, faster ships, faster trains, faster cars, faster airplanes, faster rockets. But speed without control isn’t progress; it is just a countdown to impact. Without a way to control or contain it, speed becomes the most deadly force in the universe... or one of them.

Technically, speed itself isn’t a force, and the physics make the problem even more interesting. The energy carried by a moving object increases with the square of its velocity, so if you double the speed, you haven’t merely doubled the kinetic energy that needs to be dealt with—you’ve quadrupled it. (Thank you, Ms. Wahl, my high school AP Physics teacher.) That means every great advance in acceleration eventually creates another engineering problem: how are we going to stop this thing?

01Everything Needs a Brake

Once you start looking for brakes, you realize they are everywhere. A skier turning across the fall line is effectively braking, with the edges of the skis redirecting motion and scrubbing off speed. A parachute is a brake, and so is a sea wall or breakwater, which dissipates wave energy before it reaches shore. Aircraft deploy spoilers and speed brakes to increase drag and reduce speed, spacecraft use retrograde thrust to reduce velocity, and even something as simple as dragging an object across the ground is a crude form of braking, with friction converting motion into heat.

Human beings understood the principle of resisting motion long before anyone called it a braking system. Think of the ancient Egyptians moving enormous stones and erecting monuments. It would be inaccurate to say they possessed a “brake” in the automotive sense, and historians still debate exactly how some of those enormous objects were raised, but ropes, friction, manpower and counterforce allowed heavy loads to be restrained as well as moved.

That opposing force is the important part: one group produces motion, and something else controls it. Acceleration and deceleration, push and resistance; call it engineering’s version of yin and yang.

And I have to believe that somewhere shortly after someone first looked at humanity’s newest invention—the wheel—and said, “This is fantastic,” came another person running downhill behind it screaming, “HOW DO WE STOP IT?” I doubt the wheel got many test drives before that became obvious, which means that philosophically, at least, the wheel and the brake have probably been partners from the beginning.

And having now wandered dangerously far down a philosophical road, I am going to do exactly what this article is about: brake, and talk about cars.

02The Flintstones Had It Almost Right

The most basic brake imaginable is the Flintstones solution: put your feet down, create friction and slow down. (Please do not try this in your Volvo.) But fundamentally, virtually every conventional friction brake is accomplishing the same thing. You have a rotating object, you press another material against it, and friction converts the vehicle’s kinetic energy principally into heat.

That last word, heat, is the key to nearly everything that follows. The challenge isn’t merely making a car stop once, because almost anything can stop once. The difficult part is stopping a heavy object traveling very quickly, again and again, without the braking system overheating, fading, boiling its fluid, destroying its friction material or catching something on fire. That is why automotive brake development eventually became a battle against heat.

And the amount of heat is staggering. Power is force times speed, so at the instant a typical 1,800 kg (3,968 lb) crossover begins a hard stop from 60 mph, its brakes are absorbing energy at about 426 kW (572 hp), nearly 3 times what its 200 hp engine can make. Your brakes are, by a wide margin, the most powerful thing on your car.

03Before Cars: Trains Had a Much Bigger Problem

One of the most important braking breakthroughs actually arrived before the automobile, because the railroad had a spectacular problem. A locomotive could pull a long train weighing hundreds, and eventually thousands, of tons, but early trains did not have a convenient centralized system capable of applying every brake throughout the train simultaneously. Brakemen physically operated the brakes on individual cars. Imagine the engineer realizing he needed to stop, signaling the train crew and relying on men positioned along a moving train to apply the brakes.

For decades, stopping a freight train meant brakemen running along the roofs of the moving cars, jumping the gaps between them and cranking down a hand-brake wheel on each one when the engineer whistled for brakes, in rain, in ice and in tunnel smoke. Coupling the cars together by hand was worse. By the federal government’s own count, in 1893 a trainman faced odds of 1 in 9 of being injured that year and 1 in 115 of being killed. Too bad disability insurance was not around then. Or rather, not for them: for members of the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, the union’s own death benefit was the only insurance they could get.

George Westinghouse changed that. In 1869, at only 22 years old, Westinghouse patented his compressed-air railway brake. Rather than treating every railcar as a separate braking problem, the system allowed the engineer to control braking throughout the train. His company’s history tells of an early trial run out of Pittsburgh in 1868, before the patent was even granted, that ended in an emergency stop short of a horse and wagon on the tracks, which is the kind of product demonstration you only need to do once. Westinghouse subsequently developed an automatic air-brake system as well, patented in 1872, which flipped the logic: air pressure holds the brakes off, so if a hose bursts or the train breaks in two, every brake on the train comes on by itself.

And something extremely important happened. Trains didn’t merely become better at stopping; they could become safer at going faster. The Library of Congress explicitly notes that Westinghouse’s invention made braking safer and so permitted trains to travel at higher speeds. There is the entire premise of this article in one invention: better brakes create faster vehicles.

Better brakes create faster vehicles.

04The Automobile Discovers That Going Is Easier Than Stopping

Early road vehicles used spectacularly simple technology, with a block, sometimes wood, pushed against the rotating wheel. That’s basically a horse carriage wearing brake pads on the outside, and it worked because vehicles were light and slow.

Then engines arrived. Karl Benz’s 1886 Patent-Motorwagen, the car generally credited as the first automobile, still stopped like a carriage: pull a hand lever, and a wooden block pressed against the iron rim of a rear wheel. Which is how, in August 1888, the history of the brake pad ran straight into Karl’s wife, Bertha.

Bertha took the car, and her 2 teenage sons, on the first long-distance drive in automotive history, from Mannheim to her mother’s home in Pforzheim, without bothering to tell her husband first. On the way back, at a village called Bauschlott, the wooden brake blocks were wearing away, so she found a shoemaker, named on the memorial route today as Karl Britsch, and had him nail leather onto them. Wagon builders had faced brake blocks with leather before, but nobody had done it on a car. It was the first brake lining on an automobile, and it was installed by a cobbler, at the side of the road, on a trip her husband did not know she was taking. (The rest of her remarkable story is in Forgotten Pioneers.)

After that, things moved quickly. Speeds increased, weights increased and rubber tires replaced steel-rimmed wheels, and rubbing a chunk of material against the outside of a tire stopped looking like an especially sophisticated long-term strategy. By the beginning of the 20th century, engineers were already arriving at the 2 braking architectures that remain familiar today: the drum and the disc.

05The Beat of a Different Drum, and the Disc

Renault developed an influential internally expanding drum arrangement around 1902, while British engineer Frederick William Lanchester patented an automobile disc brake during approximately the same period. Early disc technology struggled because the available friction materials and metallurgy were not yet ready for the job. Interestingly, the disc brake was not really invented “after” the drum brake. They effectively grew up together; the drum simply matured sooner.

The breakthrough came from inside the wheel. Wilhelm Maybach is usually credited with the first drum brake on a car, around 1900, and Louis Renault patented the internal expanding drum brake in 1902: 2 curved shoes, faced with friction material, sitting inside a drum that spins with the wheel. Press the pedal and the shoes push outward against the inside of the drum. By 1905 most carmakers had them. In 1908 an Englishman named Herbert Frood began weaving asbestos into brake linings, and his company, Ferodo, became so synonymous with the stuff that its name is still on brake parts today.

How a Drum Brake Works

Picture a metal bowl spinning with the wheel, with curved brake shoes inside it. Press the brake pedal, and the shoes move outward and contact the inside surface of the rotating drum, and friction slows the drum. It is simple, cheap, compact and remarkably effective.

Drums also have a useful characteristic called self-energizing action: rotation of the drum can help pull a shoe harder into the braking surface, which allows substantial stopping force without enormous hydraulic pressure.

So why did performance cars largely abandon them? Heat. The braking surfaces are enclosed inside the drum, where heat doesn’t escape particularly well, and repeated hard stops can raise temperatures enough that the coefficient of friction drops. The pedal still works, but the brakes just don’t work as well. That is brake fade, and brake fade is one of the more unpleasant phrases to discover while descending a mountain.

Still, that self-energizing trick is one engineers admire to this day. The leading shoe, the one that meets the spinning drum head-on, gets dragged into it by the rotation and presses itself harder the harder you brake. It is free power assist, courtesy of physics. That, plus the fact that a drum is cheap, sealed against dirt and makes a perfectly good parking brake, is why drums ruled the road for half a century.

For a good part of that half century, though, most cars only had brakes on 2 wheels. It took a surprisingly long time for cars to get brakes on the front wheels, because people were genuinely afraid of them. Critics argued that a locked front wheel would wreck the steering and put the car in a ditch. Once again, humans proved they can be idiots about safety, convinced that the thing that would save them was the thing that would kill them, and it would not be the last time. (The rest of that long argument is told in Cars Are Safer Now, But Is Driving?, Stand-Ins for the Living and The Second Collision.)

Then, in Britain, the dam broke. About 28 percent of British cars had 4-wheel brakes in 1924; by 1927 it was 88 percent. For a while, the cars that had them announced it: a red triangle on the back, or the letters F.W.B., told the driver behind that this car could stop a great deal faster than he could. As far as anyone can tell, no law required it. It was part courtesy and part advertisement, and it may be the only time in automotive history that cars bragged about how quickly they could stop.

06Hydraulics: Making One Human Leg Much Stronger

Early automotive brakes were mechanically connected with rods, cables and linkages: push the pedal, pull the hardware and apply the brakes. But mechanical systems introduced adjustment problems, because different wheels could receive different forces as components stretched, wore or moved.

Hydraulics provided a much more elegant answer, with pressurized, essentially incompressible brake fluid transmitting force through the system. In 1921, the Duesenberg Model A became the first production automobile to use 4-wheel hydraulic brakes, according to the American Society of Mechanical Engineers. Other concepts preceded it, but Duesenberg put 4-wheel hydraulics into a production car, and now one pedal could reliably operate brakes at all 4 wheels.

The idea had been around for a few years. Malcolm Loughead, whose family name the world knows better by its phonetic spelling, Lockheed, was granted a patent for hydraulic brakes in 1917, and in 1924 the very first Chrysler, the Chrysler Six, brought 4-wheel hydraulics to the mass market. Ford, famously stubborn, held out with mechanical brakes until 1939, advertising them in the meantime as “the safety of steel from toe to wheel.” Steel, it turned out, was not the point.

Then came 2 more problems. The first was effort: a leg can only push so hard, so carmakers added help, first a mechanical servo driven off the transmission of the 1919 Hispano-Suiza H6, then vacuum boosters that borrowed suction from the engine’s intake. That round black can behind the brake pedal of most gasoline cars is the descendant. The second was putting all your eggs in one basket. With a single hydraulic circuit, one leak could take out every brake on the car, so carmakers split the system in 2, and a federal standard made dual circuits mandatory on new American cars from January 1, 1968. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration later estimated that the change was preventing around 260 deaths and 24,000 injuries a year.

The fluid itself became something to look after, too. Ordinary brake fluid is hygroscopic, meaning it pulls moisture out of the air through hoses and seals, and every bit of water lowers its boiling point. When brake fluid boils, it turns into vapor, and vapor, unlike liquid, compresses under your foot, which is how a firm pedal turns into one that sinks toward the floor on the way down a mountain. Federal rules set a minimum boiling point for each grade, both fresh (“dry”) and after soaking up moisture (“wet”), and the gap between those 2 numbers is the whole argument for changing your fluid.

Once again, the car didn’t become faster because someone found more horsepower. It became capable of safely handling greater speed because someone found a better way to remove speed.

07Then Racing Changed Everything

This is where braking history gets really good, because racing discovered something street drivers eventually learned: if 2 cars accelerate similarly, the car that can brake later can be faster.

Jaguar and Dunlop began serious development of automotive disc brakes over the winter of 1951 and 1952, and on June 29, 1952, Stirling Moss drove a disc-brake-equipped Jaguar C-Type to victory at Reims, which Jaguar says was the first time an international motor race had been won by a car fitted with disc brakes. Then came the 1953 24 Hours of Le Mans. The Jaguars could thunder down the Mulsanne Straight at roughly 150 mph and then brake later, and repeatedly, with far less fade than their drum-braked competitors. The result? Jaguar finished first, second and fourth.

Think about that. Jaguar’s great advantage wasn’t simply that it could go faster; it could stay fast longer before the corner. Braking had become offensive rather than defensive, a concept every racing driver understands today.

08The Disc Brake Takes Over

A disc brake flips the drum concept around. Instead of hiding the friction surfaces inside a rotating cylinder, you expose a flat rotor, and a caliper straddles that rotor. Inside the caliper are brake pads, hydraulic pressure pushes pistons against the pads, the pads squeeze the rotor, and motion becomes heat.

The advantage is that the rotor lives out in the airflow, so it can cool much more effectively. Water sheds more readily, inspection is easier, and repeated high-energy braking generally produces much less fade.

In 1955, the remarkable Citroën DS brought hydraulically assisted front disc brakes into true series production, another major step toward the modern braking system. (The DS has its own story in The Goddess of Serenity, and its Maserati-powered sibling, the SM, in Her Majesty Drives Herself.) Over the following decades, front discs became normal.

The disc brake, remember, is older than most people think. Frederick Lanchester patented one in Birmingham, England, in December 1902, and it failed for reasons any modern driver would recognize: on the dusty, muddy roads of the day the pads wore away almost as fast as you could fit them, and it was noisy. The idea went back on the shelf for nearly 50 years.

When the disc came back, it came back in the unlikeliest car in America. From May 1949, every Crosley, the little economy car built by a radio magnate, came with “Hydradisc” spot disc brakes. It was a genuinely advanced idea undone by weather: road salt corroded them, and by the middle of 1950 Crosley had quietly gone back to drums. Chrysler offered a disc system of its own from late 1949, standard on the Crown Imperial into the mid-1950s, though it worked more like a pair of discs expanding inside a drum-shaped housing than anything you would recognize today.

And then, as we saw, Le Mans proved the point. Jaguar raced its C-Type with Dunlop disc brakes from the 1952 Mille Miglia, Moss won at Reims that summer, and in 1953 Tony Rolt and Duncan Hamilton won Le Mans in a disc-braked C-Type at an average of 105.85 mph, the first time anyone had won the race at more than 100 mph. The advantage was never that a disc could stop harder once. It was that it could stop just as hard the 300th time.

The reason is heat. A disc brake puts the friction outside, in the open air: a flat iron rotor spins with the wheel, and a caliper squeezes pads against both faces of it. The heat pours straight into the passing air, and when the rotor expands, it grows thicker, into the pads, rather than away from them. Water flings off it. Fade, the drum’s great weakness, very nearly disappeared.

DrumDisc
Where the friction happensShoes push outward inside a spinning drumPads squeeze both faces of an exposed rotor

09Drum Brakes Aren’t Bad

But drums never completely disappeared, and there is a reason. This distinction matters: disc brakes are not universally “better” in every possible application. Drums are cheap, they package well, they can provide strong braking force and they make an excellent parking brake. And the rear axle of an ordinary front-engine passenger car often performs substantially less braking work than the front axle, so for decades manufacturers commonly fitted front discs and rear drums, which was perfectly reasonable.

The front brakes carry much of the load because when a car decelerates, weight transfers forward. Watch a car stop hard and you will see the nose dive and the rear rise. More vertical load is now available at the front tires, allowing the front brakes to contribute more before the tires lose traction.

For a commuter car making grocery-store trips, putting giant 6-piston race brakes on the rear axle would accomplish roughly the same thing as fitting a refrigerator with a rear wing: interesting, but not particularly necessary.

10Vented, Drilled and Slotted: What Is All This Stuff?

This is where brake marketing sometimes outruns brake engineering, so it is worth looking at what each type actually is.

Solid rotors

A solid rotor is exactly what it sounds like: one solid disc. It is cheap, durable and perfectly adequate for relatively low-energy braking applications, and you will often see them on rear axles.

Vented rotors

Now imagine 2 rotor faces separated by internal cooling passages. Those passages act like a centrifugal air pump as the disc rotates, pulling air through the rotor. Venting is one of the most important developments for controlling rotor temperature, and almost every serious front brake on a performance car uses some form of ventilated rotor.

Cross-drilled rotors

Those dramatic holes running through the rotor look fantastic behind a large alloy wheel. Historically, drilling helped evacuate gases produced by older brake-pad compounds and could improve wet response and cooling behavior. But holes also remove material and create potential stress concentrations, and under extreme, repeated track use, drilled rotors can sometimes develop cracks around the holes. That doesn’t mean drilled rotors are inherently bad, since high-quality engineering, manufacturing and materials matter enormously, but “more holes” does not automatically mean “better brake.”

Slotted rotors

Slots sweep across the pad surface. They can help clear water, debris and the boundary layer created at the friction interface while maintaining a fresh braking surface, though the trade-offs can include greater pad wear and additional noise. Interestingly, even Brembo, which sells plenty of drilled discs, says slotted discs stand up to cracking better on a racetrack. So that enormous drilled-and-slotted rotor on a modified Honda may indeed be doing something. Whether the driver needed it while traveling 32 mph to Starbucks is another question.

Once the disc won, the arguments moved to the disc itself, and they have never really stopped. A rotor’s job is to be a heat sponge: soak up the energy of the stop, then get rid of it before the next one. Everything about its design is a trade between how much heat it can hold, how fast it can shed it, how much it weighs and how much it costs.

TypeWhat it isGood atThe catchTypical use
SolidOne plain iron plateCheap, thin and lightThe least able to shed heatRear axles, small cars
Vented2 faces joined by internal vanes; air pumps through the middle as it spinsFar better cooling for its weightThicker and heavier than solidFront axle of most cars
Cross-drilledHoles through the friction facesLets gas and water escape; looks fastHoles can start cracks under hard track useStreet performance
SlottedShallow grooves cut across the facesWipes the pads clean of gas, dust and water; resists crackingA little more pad wear and noiseTrack days, towing
Carbon-ceramicCarbon fiber locked in silicon carbideRoughly half the weight of iron, huge heat capacity, very long lifeVery expensive to buy and replaceSupercars, high-end performance options
Carbon-carbonCarbon fiber in a carbon matrixThe lightest; thrives at 1,000°C (1,832°F)Barely bites until it is hotFormula 1, top-level racing

Cross-drilling is the one people argue about at car meets. The holes date back to a time when pad resins gave off gas as they got hot, and a cushion of that gas between pad and disc could leave the car floating on it, so drilling gave the gas somewhere to go. Alcon, which builds racing brakes, says modern pads no longer outgas that way, that the holes are therefore unnecessary and that every one is a place for a crack to start, and it recommends slots instead. Brembo says the holes clear gas and water and actually shed heat better than slots, while agreeing that slotted discs resist cracking better on a racetrack, and calls the overall difference minimal. My rule of thumb: if you go to track days, slots. If you go to Cars and Coffee, drill away.

Fun fact

Your rotors almost certainly are not warped. That shudder through the pedal is usually uneven pad material smeared onto the disc, which leaves it microscopically thicker in some places than others. A variation of just 30 micrometers, less than half the width of a human hair, is enough to make the pedal judder; a new disc measures under 13. Push the brakes past their temperature limit and the pads deposit even more unevenly, and above about 650°C (1,202°F) the iron under those deposits can turn into cementite, a hard iron carbide that makes it worse. A genuinely bent rotor is extremely rare. It takes something like a glowing-hot disc plunged through standing water. Resurfacing hides the problem; a proper bed-in procedure prevents it.

11Then Someone Made Brakes Out of Ceramics

First, the part that actually wears out: the pad. For most of the 20th century it was made with asbestos, which the EPA finally banned from aftermarket brakes in 2024. Copper took over, until researchers found that copper washing off the roads dulls a salmon’s sense of smell, so the little leaf symbol on the box today means your brake pads are regulated for the benefit of fish. Every pad also has a happy place, a temperature window where it grips best: a street pad works on a cold morning, while a race pad is grabby and noisy until it gets properly hot.

Then there is carbon-ceramic, which has almost nothing in common with “ceramic” pads beyond the word. It is the whole rotor, made of carbon fiber locked in silicon carbide instead of cast iron, and it weighs roughly half as much. It shrugs off heat that would make iron fade, it lasts far longer, and because it cuts weight right at the wheel, the suspension has less mass to control over every bump.

The catch is the price. As a factory option on a high-performance car, carbon-ceramics typically run $8,500 to $10,000, and replacing a worn pair later can cost well into 5 figures. For everyday driving, good iron brakes are already so capable that you are paying mostly for heat capacity, weight and track stamina, not a shorter stop.

Which brings us to one of the biggest misconceptions about brakes. Brakes do not stop the car; tires do. Any modern brake system can lock the wheels, and what limits a single emergency stop is how much grip the tires have, which is why the best stopping distances ever recorded belong to cars on very sticky tires, not necessarily the cars with the most exotic brakes. Bigger brakes buy you stamina, the ability to make that same stop again and again without fading, plus better feel. They do not buy you a shorter first stop. (The tires get their own article: I’m Rubber, You’re Glue.)

12You Can Even Brake With Air

And I don’t mean air brakes on a truck; I mean literally using air to slow the car. The Bugatti Veyron is one of the best examples. Above 124 mph (200 km/h), heavy braking commands the Veyron’s rear wing to rotate dramatically upward, and the wing becomes an aerodynamic brake, creating drag while also increasing rear downforce. Bugatti says the wing moves into position in about 0.4 seconds, adding roughly 300 kg (661 lb) of rear downforce.

That produces 2 benefits. First, drag itself slows the car, and second, increased rear downforce allows the rear tires to contribute more braking force without losing traction. At high speed, Bugatti’s launch figures put the air brake alone at as much as about 0.6 g of deceleration. Suddenly the wing isn’t simply helping the car corner; it is part of the braking system.

13Air Brakes: The Other Kind

Heavy trucks use air brakes for a completely different reason. Rather than sending hydraulic fluid through the vehicle, an air-brake system stores compressed air and uses it to actuate the brakes, and commercial driver’s manuals describe it as really 3 braking systems in one: service, parking and emergency. This arrangement is extremely useful for long, heavy combination vehicles. It also integrates naturally with trailers and provides robust fail-safe possibilities through spring brakes, which clamp on by themselves if the air pressure is lost, the same lose-the-air, brakes-come-on logic Westinghouse gave the railroads.

That familiar PSHHHHHH you hear from a tractor-trailer is part of an entirely different braking world from the hydraulic system in your family car, yet both systems eventually accomplish the same thing: force friction material against a rotating surface and make heat.

14Airplanes: When the Brake Job Gets Serious

If you really want to appreciate brakes, consider an airliner aborting takeoff. In April 2026, Boeing tested exactly that with a fully loaded 737-10: it reached 207 mph, the pilots aborted the takeoff and stopped it on the wheel brakes alone, without the thrust reversers, and the brakes passed 1,371°C (2,500°F).

A brake doesn’t make energy disappear; it turns motion into heat, and that is a tremendous amount of heat. Aviation, as it happens, also taught brakes not to lock. Dunlop’s anti-skid system was stopping airliners in the early 1950s, and in 1966 the Jensen FF borrowed it to become the first production car with anti-lock brakes.

15ABS: The Computer Learns How to Brake Better Than Your Foot

For decades, drivers were taught to pump the brakes during emergency stops, because locking a wheel creates another problem: a locked tire is sliding, and a sliding tire can’t steer very effectively.

Here is the problem every driver eventually meets: stand on the brakes hard enough and the wheels lock. A locked tire slides, a sliding tire grips less than a rolling one, and a locked front wheel cannot steer, so you skid, straight on, in exactly the direction you were trying not to go. Anti-lock brakes fix that by watching each wheel and easing off the pressure the moment one starts to lock, then reapplying it, over and over, faster than any human foot could.

ABS automates the process with sensors, hydraulic valves and electronic control. The system recognizes when a wheel is approaching lockup, reduces braking pressure, allows rotation to recover and reapplies pressure extraordinarily quickly. The important benefit isn’t simply shorter stopping distances under every conceivable condition; it is maintaining directional control while braking heavily.

Bosch introduced its first production-ready electronically controlled ABS in 1978, and Mercedes-Benz offered the Bosch system on the W116 S-Class beginning that year.

ABS became the foundation for something much larger: traction control, stability control, brake assist and modern driver-assistance systems. Many of those technologies depend upon the same basic ability, individually controlling the brakes at each wheel, and the brake pedal had quietly become a computer input.

Mercedes then discovered that people in a real emergency do not press the pedal hard enough, so in December 1996 the S-Class and SL got Brake Assist, which reads how fast your foot hits the pedal and, if it looks like panic, applies full force for you. The year before, the S 600 Coupé had introduced electronic stability control, developed with Bosch, which brakes individual wheels to stop a skid before you know you are in one; it became required on new American cars from the 2012 model year.

The latest step is taking the hydraulics out altogether. Continental’s MK C1, in production since 2016, rolls the master cylinder, the booster and the stability control into a single box that builds pressure in about 150 milliseconds, roughly twice as fast as a conventional system; your pedal is now mostly a sensor. In 2026, Brembo said its Sensify system, with no hydraulic circuits at all, had gone into series production for an unnamed global automaker, and China’s new braking standard, in force since January 1, 2026, cleared the way for fully electromechanical brakes. From a cobbler’s hammer in Bauschlott to a software update in 138 years.

16And Then EVs Made Braking Produce Energy

For more than a century, braking meant turning motion into heat and throwing it away. Then electric cars turned the whole idea backward. In an EV, the motor can run as a generator when you slow down, turning the car’s motion into electricity and sending it back to the battery. That is regenerative braking. So yes, braking now charges your car. Say what?

Brake gently and regeneration does most of the work; brake hard and the regular brakes join in. The irony is that EV brakes get used so little they can rust, which is why Tesla tells owners to use them regularly. George Westinghouse would probably need a minute.

17So How Long Do Brake Pads Last?

There is no universal number. Vehicle weight, pad composition, driving style and terrain all matter, as does whether you tow, and whether the car uses regenerative braking matters enormously. AAA gives roughly 30,000 miles as a general reference point while emphasizing that driving conditions can change pad life significantly. But plenty of drivers will see dramatically more than that, and others much less. A gently driven hybrid might go an extremely long time on pads, while a 2,270 kg (5,000 lb) performance SUV repeatedly driven through mountain roads may have a different opinion.

Other sources put the typical range anywhere from 25,000 to 75,000 miles, with Kelley Blue Book’s average around 40,000. Rotors usually go 50,000 to 70,000 miles, and the front pads wear out first because the front brakes do roughly 70 percent of the work. On hybrids and EVs, owner reports of 100,000-mile pads are common, though those come from owners rather than manufacturers. Brake fluid is the exception to all of this: it goes by the calendar, and most manufacturers that set an interval say every 2 to 3 years, whatever the mileage.

Signs your brakes are asking for attention

A high-pitched squeal when you brake (many pads carry a small metal tab designed to do exactly that when they are worn), a grinding noise (metal on metal, and now it is costing you rotors), a pedal that judders, a pedal that feels soft or sinks, the car pulling to one side, or a brake warning light on the dash. None of those get better on their own.

18What Is Worse: One Hard Freeway Stop or Constant City Braking?

Over the life of the brake pads? City driving. Stop, accelerate, stop, accelerate, stop: every stop removes a tiny amount of friction material, and AAA specifically notes that frequent stop-and-go driving shortens the life of your brakes. But a single hard freeway stop can generate far more thermal stress, because the amount of kinetic energy increases dramatically with speed. So think about it this way: city driving is death by a thousand cuts, and one panic stop from 80 mph is a punch in the face.

Put numbers on it and both answers hold up. Stop for stop, the freeway is far harder. Remember the square, and the chart at the top of this article: one stop from 70 mph carries the same energy as 5.4 stops from 30 mph, and it puts all of it into the brakes in a few seconds, so the temperature spikes. Heat is what really wears a pad, and wear climbs steeply once a pad passes its comfortable temperature.

Mile for mile, the city wins, or rather loses, by a mile. On the freeway you might brake properly once every 10 miles, while in town you might stop at every block. That adds up to vastly more total energy through the brakes per mile, which is exactly why city driving is the textbook pad killer. Consider 2 numbers. The government estimates an EV recovers 32 percent of its energy through regeneration in the city and just 6 percent on the highway, which tells you how much more braking city driving involves. And in Europe, brake wear accounts for up to 55 percent of non-exhaust particle pollution in cities, but only about 3 percent on highways.

Worst of all is riding the brakes down a long mountain grade, which piles on heat with no time to cool until the brakes fade. Shift down and let the engine help.

19Different Cars Need Different Brakes

A Mazda Miata does not need the braking system from a Cayenne Turbo, a pickup towing about 5,400 kg (12,000 lb) has a different braking problem from a lightweight sports coupe, and a commuter EV has another problem entirely. A race car, meanwhile, is essentially a machine designed to repeatedly convert ridiculous amounts of speed into ridiculous amounts of heat.

Brake design therefore becomes a balancing act involving vehicle mass, maximum speed, tire grip, aerodynamic load, intended use, thermal capacity, unsprung weight, cost, pedal feel, noise, dust, durability and packaging. The biggest brake isn’t automatically the best brake; the correct brake is the brake engineered for the energy the vehicle must repeatedly manage.

A note on calipers, since the table mentions them. A floating caliper has pistons on one side only and slides on pins to squeeze both pads, which makes it cheap, compact and perfectly good for most cars. A fixed caliper is bolted solid and has pistons on both sides, often 4, 6 or more, giving more even pressure and a firmer pedal. That is what is hiding behind the bright red paint.

20The Technology That Lets Us Go Faster

We celebrate horsepower, zero-to-60 times and top speed, but we almost never see a car advertisement screaming “60 TO ZERO!” Perhaps we should. Nearly every leap forward in transportation has needed someone to solve the opposite problem: Westinghouse’s air brake let trains run faster, hydraulics let cars get heavier and quicker, disc brakes let Jaguars brake later at Le Mans and ABS let drivers steer at the limit.

Acceleration gets all the glory, but braking makes acceleration possible. It is the counterweight, the thing that lets us approach the limit because we know there is a way back. Speed is great, but it is only worth having if you can give it back. Yin and yang; the go and the whoa.

Which brings us, somewhat improbably, back to Chris Farley and a model car on fire. His demonstration was ridiculous and the sales meeting went terribly, but the message was right. You can spend all the money in the world making something faster, but eventually you’re going to need to stop it. So buy good pads and change the fluid, because when that moment arrives, you really don’t want to discover that you bought the other guy’s brake pads.
